title: Gears and wheels
target: Use gear ratio and wheel circumference to predict an ideal travel speed.
criteria: Connect gear teeth with speed ratio.
Explain the tradeoff between ideal speed and available torque.

authoring.limitations: Reasoning evidence only. Multiple choice does not certify physical performance. Teacher reviews before assigning and rates mastery separately.

cpa.prompt: A 12-tooth driver turns a 36-tooth axle gear at 450 driver rpm. What is axle rpm?
cpa.guide: Axle rpm = driver rpm × driver teeth / driven teeth = 450/3 = 150.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: A motor gear drives a gear with four times as many teeth. In an ideal lossless pair, which comparison is correct?
options: Axle rate quadruples; torque is unchanged.
Axle rate and torque both quadruple.
Axle rate is one-quarter; axle torque is four times the input torque.
Rate and torque are both unchanged.
cpa.guide: The 4:1 reduction trades speed for torque; it does not multiply power.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Compare evidence and identify a physical relationship.

cpa.prompt: A no-slip wheel has circumference 0.24 m and turns at 90 rpm. What is ideal ground speed?
cpa.guide: 90 rpm = 1.5 revolutions per second. Multiply circumference by 1.5; do not treat minutes as seconds.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: A wheel diameter is 0.10 m. Use π = 3.14. How far does it travel in two complete turns without slipping?
cpa.guide: One circumference is πd = 0.314 m; two turns cover 0.628 m.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: At fixed axle torque, a larger wheel radius gives what ideal driving force at the ground?
options: The same force regardless of radius.
A larger force because radius always increases torque.
Zero force for every larger wheel.
A smaller force because F = torque/radius.
cpa.guide: At a fixed axle torque, increasing radius reduces tangential driving force. This explains the starting-effort tradeoff.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Compare evidence and identify a physical relationship.

cpa.prompt: A team doubles wheel diameter and predicts twice the speed. Which condition is needed for that ideal prediction?
options: The axle rate stays the same and the wheels do not slip.
The larger wheels must eliminate all losses.
The motor has no energy source.
cpa.guide: Speed is circumference × axle rate. The diameter change doubles circumference only; real loading may change axle rate.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Select a claim supported by the stated evidence and assumptions.
